options: Earth spinning on its own axis
questions.explanation: Rotation is Earth spinning in place around its own axis — one full spin takes about 24 hours and is what gives us day and night.
questions.misconception: "Rotation" and "revolution" get swapped constantly because both describe circular motion. Rotation is always the spin-in-place motion — think of a rotating fan blade.

questions.explanation: Revolution is Earth travelling all the way around the Sun — one full lap takes about 365.25 days, which defines a year.
questions.misconception: Because "revolution" sounds dramatic, it's sometimes guessed as the faster motion. It's actually the much slower, much bigger one — a full year, not a full day.

questions.prompt: About how long does one Earth rotation take?
questions.explanation: One rotation — one full spin on the axis — takes about 24 hours, which is exactly what defines a single day.
questions.misconception: 27 days is the Moon's orbital period around Earth, not Earth's own spin — an easy mix-up since both involve Earth as a reference point.

questions.prompt: Which motion is responsible for day and night?
questions.explanation: Rotation constantly turns a new part of Earth to face the Sun and turns the previous part away — that's what creates the day/night cycle every 24 hours.
questions.misconception: Revolution changes the season over a year, not the time of day — it happens far too slowly to explain something that repeats every 24 hours.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many times does Earth rotate during one full revolution around the Sun?
questions.explanation: Earth spins about 365.25 times during the same stretch of time it takes to complete one lap around the Sun — that's exactly why a calendar year has about 365 days.
questions.misconception: The numbers 24 (hours in a day) and 365 (days in a year) can feel like unrelated facts to memorize, but they're really the same two motions — rotation and revolution — compared at different timescales.
